What persists when a body meets an obstacle?

A Lenia body can keep moving and hold together for thousands of steps in an empty arena, which makes it tempting to regard its form as something robust, but what happens when we put an obstacle in its way? We compared five bodies with unobstructed copies of themselves, arranging three encounters for each, and found responses ranging from reduced progress with a modest deflection to a near-reversal accompanied by matter separating from the largest connected part. Following both motion and connectedness lets us ask how much of the encounter changes where the body goes and how much changes the organization we were recognizing as a body in the first place. This pilot leaves recovery open, because the obstacle remained throughout the observation.

How much of the body holds together?

Across all fifteen encounters, the median straight-line displacement was 18% of the unobstructed value and the median difference in direction was 26°, but those summaries hide rather different things happening to the bodies. Two kept roughly 30% of their unobstructed displacement with modest deflections, whereas another nearly reversed direction in one encounter while a substantial share of its matter separated from the largest connected part. Almost all the matter remained in the arena, so following its total alone would have missed the change in where it went and whether it stayed together.

Because the paired branches begin from the same state, their divergence measures the effect of adding the obstacle under this protocol. The obstacle acts directly on the local flow field. Whether the body’s prior shape, internal dynamics, or persistence helps predict the resulting response remains a separate question, for which these trials supply outcomes rather than a fitted model.

Finding bodies that persist while moving

The qualification screen draws on sixteen campaigns that searched for persistence, locomotion, compactness, or shape preservation. Each of their 626 exported states was replayed for 3,600 steps, measuring the body across all state channels so that a stable-looking part could not conceal changes elsewhere in the field.

Of these replays, 184 passed the temporal-individuality criterion and nine also moved at least half a body diameter. The nine qualified movers came from four discovery campaigns and travelled between 0.59 and 2.09 body diameters. Requiring persistence as well as displacement gives us bodies whose response can be compared with an established pattern of motion, rather than treating any moving fragment as a suitable specimen.

What counts as the same body over time?

For this screen, persistence means that a localized, connected body retains its organization over time. The temporal-individuality score takes the minimum of five measurements: localization, connected-body coherence, registered shape persistence, persistence of internal parts, and stability of extent. Taking the weakest score prevents strong performance on one measure from compensating for failure on another. A specimen must score at least 0.7 and pass the occupancy criteria before the displacement threshold is applied; this is an operational selection rule, not a definition of life.

One saved body, four possible continuations

An obstacle must start outside the body and still lie somewhere the body will reach. Several specimens filled too much of their native 128 × 128 or 256 × 256 arena to meet both conditions, so their saved state patches were recentered, without rescaling, in a 512 × 512 wall arena. The patches retained their original rule parameters and two state channels, including the 5 × 5 connectivity between each channel pair, time step, and reintegration settings.

After 1,200 steps, the body’s displacement over the preceding 400 steps defined its heading and the simulation state was saved. An unobstructed continuation over the next 3,600 steps then identified a future position at which all three obstacle placements—ahead, left, and right—could start clear of the body and later intersect its path. Each exposed branch began from that same saved state. The circular obstacle had half the body’s 95% mass radius and acted through an external wall potential; it neither removed matter nor introduced a sensor channel. Its position was chosen using the sham trajectory, so these are deliberately arranged encounters rather than a test of success at navigating an unknown arena.

Similar displacement losses can conceal different responses

The two highest-scoring specimens, 870DA94A and 781D0200, retained median displacements of 30% and 29% of their respective shams, with median direction differences of 13° and 12°. The other three retained 9–17% and had larger median direction differences. Those summaries conceal an important distinction: AE9700F0 and FF41DAF6 ended with a larger fraction of their matter in the dominant component than their shams, whereas B26ADEF3 had a fraction about 0.245 lower than its sham. Its ahead placement also produced the near-reversal, a response that the three-placement median alone would obscure.

The ordering suggests a question about robustness, but it does not establish that a higher temporal-individuality score causes or predicts a smaller response. These five specimens come from only two related rule families, and a small net displacement can result from turning or returning as well as from slowing. A larger comparison needs to distinguish these possibilities while separating the contribution of prior coherence from that of the generating rule.

What would a map of responses need to explain?

A single outcome label would collapse differences that matter here. Conserving total matter does not guarantee that the same connected body persists, and a small net displacement does not tell us whether a body stopped, turned, or returned toward its starting point. Displacement, direction, and connected-body coherence therefore need to remain separate outcomes if we want to understand how form relates to response.

The side placements make this distinction especially clear. Of the ten exposed branches with an obstacle to one side, four had lateral displacement away from that side and six toward it. These counts describe the final displacement, not an inferred attempt to avoid the obstacle. Shape, internal flow, and handedness could each contribute to the directional differences, but the assay does not separate them. Mirroring the initial state would test whether the bias reverses with the body; distinguishing geometry from internal flow would require further interventions.

With five specimens from two related rule families, we cannot yet determine whether similar responses occupy a connected region of the morphospace. The present experiment instead specifies quantities that a future map could predict: displacement relative to an undisturbed continuation, signed lateral displacement, direction change, and coherence change. Recovery time would add a further dimension once trials include an obstacle-removal phase. Testing predictions on held-out rule families would then show whether the relationship extends beyond close relatives of the training specimens.

Four movers could not enter the paired comparison

Of the nine qualified movers, two never reached a sham position where all three obstacles could begin clear and later intersect the body, and one moved too little during the 400-step heading window. A fourth exceeded the protocol’s limit on the radius containing 99% of its matter, even in the enlarged arena. These four were excluded before a valid paired encounter, so they contribute neither obstacle responses nor nonresponses to the results above.

The radius exclusion also raises a measurement question. A low-density halo can extend well beyond a compact core and dominate the radius needed to contain 99% of the matter. Separating core and halo measurements would help determine whether this exclusion reflects loss of a coherent body or simply a mismatch between that body and the arena-size criterion.

Can a disturbed body recover its organization?

To find out whether a body can recover after contact ends, the follow-up removes the obstacle and tracks the subsequent dynamics, separating changes that persist from responses maintained by the obstacle itself. Its results and controls are developed in the private recovery report, while the fifteen encounters above remain the evidence for this earlier comparison.

Experiment results: 2 September 2026. Prose revised and saved-result summary rechecked: 24 September 2026. The qualification screen used 626 exact replay bundles from sixteen later Flow Lenia campaigns. The assay used a 512² wall arena, two state channels, the specimens’ original 5×5 channel connectivity, a 1,200-step checkpoint, and a 3,600-step paired continuation. Claims above are descriptive for five organisms and fifteen exposed branches; no predictive model was fitted.

For the broader distinction between a disturbance and the response it produces, see developmental susceptibility. This five-body obstacle assay establishes differences in response within its tested cohort; it does not by itself establish adaptation or recovery after obstacle removal.

The follow-up experiments are complete and the new argument is drafted in the private recovery report, revision 015. This page preserves the original five-body pilot while the new evidence is reviewed; its endpoint statistics are background for the revised article.
